definitions.definition: A mapping between two things that shows they have the same structure or pattern, even if they look different on the surface.
definitions.example: A map of a subway system is isomorphic to the actual subway lines because the connections between stations are the same, even though the map is not the real thing.

definitions.definition: The study of the church, its nature, structure, and purpose.
definitions.example: Ecclesiology asks questions like 'What is the church supposed to be like?' and 'How should it be organized?'

definitions.definition: A branch of mathematics that studies networks made of points (nodes) and the lines (edges) connecting them.
definitions.example: Graph theory is used to model social networks like Facebook, where people are nodes and friendships are edges.

definitions.definition: A type of network where most nodes are not directly connected, but any two nodes can be reached through a surprisingly short chain of connections.
definitions.example: The idea that you are only six handshakes away from anyone on Earth is a small-world network property.

definitions.definition: A process where new nodes in a network are more likely to connect to nodes that already have many connections, like 'the rich get richer'.
definitions.example: On YouTube, a new video is more likely to be linked to a popular channel with millions of subscribers than to a channel with only a few.

definitions.definition: A network where a few nodes (hubs) have a huge number of connections, while most nodes have very few, following a power-law distribution.
definitions.example: The internet is a scale-free network: a few websites like Google have billions of links, while most websites have only a few.

definitions.definition: The ability of a network to keep working even when some of its parts are removed or fail.
definitions.example: A rope made of many strands is resilient because if one strand breaks, the rope still holds.

definitions.definition: A situation where the failure of one part of a network causes a chain reaction of failures in other parts.
definitions.example: When a power plant goes offline, it can cause other plants to overload and shut down, leading to a widespread blackout.

definitions.definition: The second part of the Christian Bible, containing writings about the life of Jesus and the early church.
definitions.example: The New Testament includes the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John) and letters from apostles like Paul.

definitions.definition: Special abilities given by the Holy Spirit to Christians to help serve the church and others.
definitions.example: Some spiritual gifts include teaching, healing, leadership, and showing mercy.

definitions.definition: Hostility or mistreatment directed at people because of their beliefs, especially religious beliefs.
definitions.example: In ancient Rome, Christians were sometimes thrown to lions because of their faith.

definitions.definition: The average number of steps along the shortest paths for all pairs of nodes in a network.
definitions.example: In a friend network, the average path length is the average number of 'friend-of-a-friend' connections between any two people.

definitions.definition: The tendency for nodes in a network to form tightly knit groups where many connections exist within the group.
definitions.example: In a school, a group of friends who all know each other is a cluster.

definitions.definition: A description of how many connections (degrees) each node in a network has, often shown as a graph.
definitions.example: In a social network, the degree distribution shows how many people have 1 friend, 10 friends, 100 friends, etc.

definitions.definition: A mathematical relationship where a few events are very common and many events are very rare, following a specific pattern.
definitions.example: Earthquakes follow a power-law: a few huge earthquakes happen, but thousands of tiny ones happen all the time.

definitions.definition: Nodes in a network that have a very high number of connections, acting as central points.
definitions.example: An airport like Atlanta is a hub because it connects flights from many smaller airports.

definitions.definition: When parts of a network break down by chance, without targeting any specific part.
definitions.example: If a few random streetlights go out in a city, the traffic network still works fine.

definitions.definition: When someone deliberately removes or disables the most connected nodes in a network to cause maximum damage.
definitions.example: If a hacker takes down Google, it would disrupt the internet much more than taking down a small blog.

definitions.definition: Relating to the apostles, the first leaders sent out by Jesus to spread the Christian message.
definitions.example: The apostolic church refers to the early church led by the apostles like Peter and Paul.

definitions.definition: In a way that is larger or smaller than expected based on size or importance.
definitions.example: In a game, the best player might score disproportionately more points than the rest of the team.

definitions.definition: A measure of how connected the neighbors of a node are to each other, indicating how 'cliquey' a network is.
definitions.example: If all your friends also know each other, your clustering coefficient is high.

definitions.definition: The point at which a network breaks apart into isolated pieces when nodes are removed.
definitions.example: If you remove enough roads from a city map, eventually you can't drive from one side to the other — that's the percolation threshold.

definitions.definition: Connections between different groups in a network that link otherwise separate clusters.
definitions.example: A student who is friends with both the jocks and the nerds is a bridge tie between those groups.

definitions.definition: The process by which information spreads through a network from person to person.
definitions.example: A rumor spreading through a school is an example of information diffusion.

definitions.definition: Information that is already known or repeated, providing no new knowledge.
definitions.example: If your friend tells you the same joke you already heard, that's redundant information.

definitions.definition: Traveling from place to place, especially for work or religious purposes.
definitions.example: An itinerant preacher travels to different towns to give sermons.

definitions.definition: The longest shortest path between any two nodes in a network, measuring the network's overall size.
definitions.example: In a social network, the network diameter is the maximum number of handshakes needed to connect any two people.

definitions.definition: The study of how parts of a network are arranged and connected, focusing on shape and structure rather than exact positions.
definitions.example: The topology of a subway map shows which stations connect to which, not the exact geographic locations.

definitions.definition: Able to be checked or proven through observation or experiment.
definitions.example: The claim that water boils at 100°C is empirically verifiable by heating water and measuring its temperature.

definitions.definition: Relating to the study of society, social groups, and human relationships.
definitions.example: A sociological study might look at how friendships form in a school.

definitions.definition: A table used to show which nodes in a network are connected to each other, with rows and columns representing nodes.
definitions.example: In a class of 5 students, an adjacency matrix would have a 1 if two students are friends and a 0 if they are not.

definitions.definition: A type of mapping where the underlying structure or pattern is the same between two systems, even if the details differ.
definitions.example: A chessboard and a checkerboard have a structural isomorphism because both are 8x8 grids with alternating colors.

definitions.definition: The study of how diseases spread and affect populations.
definitions.example: Epidemiology helped scientists understand how COVID-19 spread from person to person.

definitions.definition: Growing naturally and without artificial or external control, like a plant growing from a seed.
definitions.example: An organic friendship develops naturally over time, not because someone forces it.

definitions.definition: Relating to an established organization or system with formal rules and structures.
definitions.example: An institutional church has a formal hierarchy like bishops and parishes.

definitions.definition: A series of events that happen one after another, often spreading like a waterfall.
definitions.example: A cascade of applause starts when one person claps and then everyone joins in.

definitions.definition: The act of abandoning or renouncing one's religious faith.
definitions.example: If a Christian decides to stop believing in God and leaves the church, that is apostasy.

definitions.definition: The process of proving a theory or claim wrong by finding evidence that contradicts it.
definitions.example: The theory that all swans are white was falsified when black swans were discovered in Australia.

definitions.definition: A close similarity or connection between two things.
definitions.example: There is a correspondence between the keys on a piano and the notes they produce.

definitions.definition: A statement or principle that is accepted as true without needing proof, serving as a starting point for reasoning.
definitions.example: In geometry, 'a straight line is the shortest distance between two points' is an axiom.

definitions.definition: The process of coming together or moving toward a common point or result.
definitions.example: Multiple streams converging into a single river is a physical example of convergence.

definitions.definition: The state of not being complete or whole; in logic, the idea that some truths cannot be proven within a system.
definitions.example: A puzzle with missing pieces has incompleteness.

definitions.definition: Unearned favor or kindness from God, often seen as a free gift.
definitions.example: Grace is like a teacher giving a student an 'A' not because the student earned it, but out of kindness.

definitions.definition: A measure of disorder or randomness in a system; things tend to become more disordered over time.
definitions.example: A messy bedroom has higher entropy than a tidy one, and it naturally gets messier without effort.

definitions.definition: The process by which a quantum system loses its quantum properties and behaves classically, often due to interaction with the environment.
definitions.example: Decoherence is like a spinning top that slowly wobbles and stops due to friction with the air.

definitions.definition: The quality of being logical, consistent, and forming a unified whole; in physics, waves that are in step with each other.
definitions.example: A choir singing in harmony has coherence; a crowd shouting randomly does not.
